persona.bio: Jess, 29, event coordinator at a restaurant group in Chicago. Her Gmail inbox is full of clients, caterers, florists and AV people. She keeps the run of show, floor plans and vendor timelines in Google Sheets, collects headcounts and dietary lists the week before each event, and is on site with a headset on event nights. Vendor follow ups eat her afternoons, and she loses track of who hasn't replied. She uses ChatGPT a few times a week for emails. Her company is fine with AI and IT said she can connect ChatGPT to her work Gmail.

steps.note: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group in Chicago. I plan private events and run them on the night. I write to clients planning an event, to vendors, and to my own kitchen and floor team. My tone is warm, clear and direct, and I keep emails short, usually a few sentences. I put the date and what I need first, then the deadline. Never add details I did not give you, like prices, headcounts, menus or policies. If something is missing, leave a square bracket for me to fill in. Give me one draft at a time, and I will read it and change it before anything goes out.

steps.task: Follow up emails to vendors and clients
steps.title: Your follow up emails, drafted from your inbox for your OK
steps.read: Your follow ups are drafted from your Gmail by ChatGPT, and each one waits for your OK. You stop starting every vendor and client chase from a blank page. The draft goes to the right person about the right event, and you decide what gets sent.

material.label: Instructions for your assistant
items: I’m an event coordinator for a restaurant group in Chicago. I plan private events and run them on the night. Look in my Gmail for threads where I asked a vendor or client for something and they have not answered. That includes final headcounts, dietary lists, deposits, signed contracts, delivery times and menu choices. Count a thread as waiting when my message was the last one and [number] days have passed. If the event is within a week, count it as waiting sooner. For each waiting thread, write a short follow up in my voice. Be warm, direct and brief. Put the event date and what I need first, then the deadline. Never add details I did not give you, like prices, numbers or policies. Use a square bracket where something is missing. Give me one draft per thread, with the person’s role and the event name above it, and wait for me to read it. Do not send anything.

material.label: Your follow up wording
items: First nudge: Hi [first name], just checking in on [what I need] for [event name] on [date]. I need it by [deadline] so we can plan on our end. Let me know if anything is holding it up. Thanks!

Second nudge: Hi [first name], following up again on [what I need] for [event name] on [date]. We are getting close, and I need it by [deadline] to keep everything on track. Can you send it today, or call me at [phone] if it is easier? Thank you!

steps.title: Answering messages, drafted in your inbox
steps.read: Reply drafts appear right inside Gmail, so you answer from the email itself. You type what you mean in a few words, Help me write turns it into a draft, and you check it before you send. Your replies stay in your voice and your details stay yours.

material.label: Starting lines for replies
items: Thank [first name] for the update on [event name]. Confirm I have the headcount of [number] and ask for the dietary list by [day].
Tell the client we received their deposit for [event name] on [date] and the date is held. Say I will send the next details by [day].
Ask the vendor to confirm delivery time of [time] on [date] at [location], and ask who will be on site.
Tell the client the menu choices are due by [day] so the kitchen can plan. Offer a quick call at [day and time] if they have questions.
Reply that I can’t promise [request] yet. Say I am checking with [role] and will answer by [day].
Thank the guest for their message and say I will pass the request to the kitchen. Ask them to confirm [detail].
Ask the team to confirm arrival time of [time] for the event on [date] and reply with any questions by [day].

material.label: Notes on your tone
items: If the draft sounds stiff with a client who is already friendly, press Friendly.
If it sounds too casual for a first message to a new client or a formal request, press Formalize.
If it runs long for a vendor or a quick confirmation, press Shorten.
If a draft adds a detail I did not give, fix it or delete the line before sending. I read everything first.

safeUse: Never type guest names, phone numbers, home addresses or payment details into a chat tool. Use square brackets instead.
Leave out allergy details tied to a named guest. Say ’one guest with a nut allergy’ without naming the person.
Do not paste contracts, deposit amounts or card numbers. Add those yourself after the draft.
Check every date, headcount, time and menu item against your own sheet before you send.
Read every draft before it goes out. You send it, never the tool.
steps.askMessage: Hi [manager’s name], I’m using AI to speed up the writing side of my event work and want to make sure I stay within company rules. Which AI tools are approved, and what may I use them for? I have in mind drafting follow up emails to vendors and clients, and drafting replies to messages in Gmail. I would link my work email to ChatGPT for the follow ups, with every draft waiting for my OK before anything is sent. Could you let me know what is allowed, or point me to the right person?

design.task: Follow up emails to vendors and clients
design.today: You write these a few times a week, often from scratch. Vendor follow ups eat your afternoons, and you chase final numbers across Gmail threads, texts, Google Sheets and phone calls.
design.newWay: Once a week a list of who has not answered you shows up, read only from your Gmail. For the people you decide to chase, your AI tool drafts each follow up from the thread, using your saved tone notes, and you read it before it goes. You stop writing from scratch and stop hunting through threads to see who still owes you a headcount or a dietary list.

steps.goal: Get ChatGPT ready on your phone and computer so the same tool is there wherever you work.
Save instructions about your role, your restaurant group and how you like to sound so every draft starts from your voice.
Make one project for event follow ups that holds your tone notes and a few of your past follow ups as examples.
Set up a weekly list of vendors and clients who have not answered you, read from Gmail without sending anything.
Have drafts for the people you pick written from their Gmail threads, with the tool asking before it sends anything.
Decide which details every follow up must state, such as event date, final headcount and dietary list deadline.

For messages that need more thought, you say what you want to tell them out loud and get finished text back in your voice. You still decide every answer, but you stop retyping the same ones.

material.label: Example run of show

material.label: Event details form
material.what: A short list of what to paste in each time: date, guest count, room, vendors, timings and special requests.

design2.checkPoint: You read the run of show and check every time, name, number and vendor arrival before you share it with the team.

design2.today: You put these together for each event. The numbers come from Gmail threads, texts and Google Sheets.
design2.newWay: You paste your messy notes, such as dietary replies, headcounts or vendor lists, and the assistant turns them into a clean table. You review the table and bring it into Google Sheets. Final numbers end up in one place, not scattered across threads and texts.

steps.goal: Get Claude ready on your phone and computer to turn notes into tables.
Turn pasted notes into a clean table with set columns and bring it into your Google Sheet.

material.label: Table instructions
material.what: The columns you want for each list type, such as guest name, dietary need, headcount and vendor status.

material.label: Notes paste prompt
material.what: A prompt that takes messy notes and returns a table ready for Sheets, marking anything unclear instead of guessing.

design2.checkPoint: You compare the table with your original notes before you import it into your sheet.

design2.today: You make these calls yourself each week.
design2.newWay: This stays yours. Calls with vendors rely on your relationships, your tone and quick decisions while you talk, and AI would not make them better. The follow up emails and lists around the calls are where your time can be saved.
design2.checkPoint: Nothing to check, because this task stays with you.
